l: yoke of the king of Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_made_of iron [placed on all these nations] Hananiah claimed the LORD had broken the yoke of the king of Babylon and would break it from all nations within two years. The LORD countered through Jeremiah that he had put a yoke of iron on all these nations so they would serve Nebuchadnezzar.

l: bar (Jeremiah's neck bar), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The bar on Jeremiah's neck was taken off and broken by Hananiah in front of the people as a sign of his prophecy. The LORD said the broken wooden bars were replaced by bars of iron.

l: Hananiah's prophecy of peace, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_a false prophecy [LORD has not sent Hananiah] Hananiah's prophecy promised that within two full years the vessels, Jeconiah, and all the captives would return from Babylon. Jeremiah said it would be tested by whether it happened, and the LORD called it a lie and rebellion, with Hananiah dying that same year.

l: Jeremiah's letter, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah's letter, carried to Babylon by Elasah and Gemariah, sent by Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar, addresses the captive elders, priests, prophets and people. It urges them to settle, multiply, seek Babylon's peace, ignore false prophets, and expect return; Shemaiah later cites it to rebuke Jeremiah.

l: deportations of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The deportations of Judah were the carrying away of its people by Nebuchadnezzar, totaling 4,600: 3,023 Jews in his seventh year, 832 persons from Jerusalem in his eighteenth, and 745 in his twenty-third under Nebuzaradan. Jeremiah instructed the captives to settle in Babylon: build, plant, marry, multiply, pray for the city, and ignore false prophets, diviners, and dreams. The LORD promised to hear them and gather them from all nations.

l: false prophets and diviners, The Book of Jeremiah
s: prophesy_falsely_in the LORD [name; not sent by the LORD] The captives are warned that the prophets and diviners among them prophesy falsely in the LORD's name, though he did not send them. Ahab, Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, and Shemaiah are named as examples. The LORD says earlier prophets he sent were not listened to, and the people's claim that he raised up prophets in Babylon is rebuked.

l: return from captivity, The Book of Jeremiah
s: occurs_after seventy years [accomplished for Babylon] The LORD promises to turn again the captivity, gather the exiles from all nations and places where he drove them, and bring them back to the place they were carried from. This follows seventy years and depends on them calling on him and seeking him with all their heart. Shemaiah will not see the good the LORD will do for his people.

l: people remaining in Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The people remaining in Jerusalem, including King Zedekiah on David's throne and brothers not taken to Babylon, are destined for divine judgment by sword, famine, and pestilence. They become like rotten figs, scattered among kingdoms as horror and reproach for ignoring prophets.

l: Ahab the son of Kolaiah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Ahab, son of Kolaiah, is a false prophet who prophesies a lie in the LORD's name and commits adultery with neighbors' wives. The LORD will deliver him to Nebuchadnezzar, who will roast him in fire before the captives, making his fate an exiles' curse formula.

l: Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, a false prophet named with Ahab, prophesied lies in the LORD's name and committed adultery with neighbors' wives; the LORD will deliver him to Nebuchadnezzar, who will kill him before the captives, making him a curse.

l: Shemaiah the Nehelamite, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Shemaiah the Nehelamite sends letters in his own name to Zephaniah and the Jerusalem priests, urging them to put Jeremiah in stocks and shackles as a madman posing as a prophet. The LORD declares he prophesied unsent and spread a lie, so he and his offspring will be punished and not see the good.

l: Jeremiah's instructions to settle in Babylon, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD's instructions to the exiles in Babylon: build houses, plant gardens, marry, have children and multiply, and seek and pray for the city's peace. Shemaiah later quotes them in his complaint against Jeremiah.

l: restoration (of Israel), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD promises Israel's restoration: breaking yokes and ending foreign enslavement, healing wounds, rebuilding the city and palace in place, bringing thanksgiving, multiplying and glorifying the people, establishing their congregation, and raising a prince from among them, drawn near to the LORD.

l: time of Jacob's trouble, The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_characterized_as great day [none is like it] The day is described as great, with none like it, marked by a voice of trembling and fear, and men with hands on their waists like a woman in labor with faces turned pale. It is called the time of Jacob's trouble, but Jacob will be saved out of it. On that day the LORD will break the yoke from the neck and burst the bonds.

l: enemies and oppressors (of Israel), The Book of Jeremiah
s: will_become plunder and prey [reversal of their fortunes] Strangers who have made Israel bondservants will do so no more, as the LORD breaks their yoke. All who devour, plunder, and prey on Israel will be devoured, plundered, and made prey, and all adversaries will go into captivity. The LORD says he will punish all who oppress them and make a full end of the nations where he scattered Israel, and his wrath will burst on the head of the wicked.

l: wound (Israel's incurable wound), The Book of Jeremiah
s: Israel's wound is declared incurable and grievous, caused by its iniquity, with no advocate or remedy and abandoned by lovers; the LORD says he inflicted it as an enemy's blow, yet promises restoration and healing for outcast Zion.

l: iniquity (Israel's sin), The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_property great [sins have increased] The text states twice that the greatness of Israel's iniquity and the increase of its sins is the reason the LORD wounded and chastised it. This is given as the reason Israel's pain is incurable and should not be cried over. The LORD says he will correct Israel in measure and will in no way leave it unpunished.

l: new covenant, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The new covenant is a promise declared by the LORD in Chapter 31, made with the houses of Israel and Judah. Unlike the broken covenant made when their fathers left Egypt, it places his law in their inward parts, writes it on their hearts, lets all know him, and forgives iniquity, remembering sin no more.

Hanamel, son of Shallum and Jeremiah's cousin, owns a field at Anathoth. As the LORD foretold, he comes to Jeremiah in the guard's court, asks him to redeem it, and witnesses the deed's delivery to Baruch.

l: Baruch the son of Neriah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Baruch, son of Neriah (and of Mahseiah), is a scribe who serves Jeremiah. He receives the sealed and open deeds of purchase before witnesses and is commanded to store them in an earthen vessel so they last many days. He writes Jeremiah's dictated words on a scroll, reads it in the LORD's house and before the princes, is told to hide, is targeted by the king, is hidden by the LORD, and writes a second scroll. The LORD speaks of sorrow added to his pain, tells him not to seek great things for himself, and promises he will escape with his life. Later he is accused of turning Jeremiah against the people and is taken into Egypt, arriving at Tahpanhes.

l: people of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: practices idolatry and child sacrifice [high places of Baal in the valley of the son of Hinnom] The people of Judah, with their kings, princes, priests, and prophets, are charged with turning their backs on the LORD, ignoring his teaching, defiling his house with abominations, and building high places of Baal in the valley of the son of Hinnom to pass their children through fire to Molech. The LORD promises that they will be regathered, given one heart, and planted in the land, and that their captivity will be reversed.
Jews scattered in Moab, Ammon, Edom and other countries hear Babylon's king left a remnant under Gedaliah, return to Judah and Gedaliah at Mizpah, and gather abundant wine and summer fruits.

l: court of the guard, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The court of the guard is where Zedekiah commands Jeremiah to be committed after the appeal. Jeremiah receives a daily loaf of bread from the bakers' street and remains there until all the city's bread is gone.

l: field at Anathoth, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A field at Anathoth in Benjamin, belonging to Hanamel, offered to Jeremiah by right of redemption and bought for seventeen shekels of silver, serving as a sign that fields will again be purchased despite Chaldean conquest.

l: deed of purchase, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A deed of purchase made in two copies, one sealed with terms and conditions and one open. Jeremiah signs, seals and witnesses it, then gives it to Baruch to store in an earthen vessel, lasting many days as a sign that property will be bought again.

l: restoration of the captivity, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The restoration of the captivity is the LORD's promise to reverse the exile of Judah and Israel. It begins with pledges to gather scattered people from all countries, resettle them safely, give them one heart, and make an everlasting covenant of good. It then moves to concrete signs: fields bought, deeds signed and sealed, and witnesses called across Benjamin and Judah. It closes by returning things to how they were at first, with joy, thanksgiving in the LORD's house, flocks in the cities, and mercy on Jacob's and David's offspring.

l: Levitical priests, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Levitical priests are ministers of the LORD. In Chapter 33 he promises they will always have a man before him offering burnt, meal, and continual sacrifices, and that he will multiply the Levites.

l: covenant of day and night, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD points to his covenant of day and night as the guarantee of his covenant with David and the Levitical priests: only if it could be broken could those covenants be broken. He repeats that if it fails, he would cast away the offspring of Jacob and David, but he will instead reverse their captivity and have mercy.

l: Babylon's army, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Babylon's army is a vast invading force under Nebuchadnezzar. It attacks Jerusalem and Judah's remaining cities, withdraws, then is commanded by the LORD to return, take and burn the city. It besieges Jerusalem, breaches it, and its princes sit in the middle gate. It is later portrayed as innumerable northern invaders delivering Egypt into its hand.

l: people of Jerusalem and Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: break covenant of liberty for servants [re-enslaved freed servants] The princes and people entered the covenant and at first obeyed by freeing their Hebrew male and female servants, but afterwards turned and forced them back into servitude. The LORD accuses them of profaning his name and breaking the covenant made by passing between the parts of a cut calf, and declares they will be given to their enemies, with their dead bodies becoming food for birds and animals.

l: servants (Hebrew bondservants), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The Hebrew male and female servants were released under the covenant so that no one would keep a fellow Jew as a bondservant. After they were let go, their masters caused them to return and brought them back into subjection as servants and handmaids.

l: covenant of liberty for servants, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A covenant Zedekiah made with all the people in Jerusalem, before the LORD in the house called by his name, to free every Hebrew male and female servant. It echoes the exodus covenant of release after seven years. The people broke it by retaking servants, bringing judgment on the covenant-breakers.

The Rechabites are a nomadic group bound by Jonadab's commands: no wine, no houses, fields, vineyards or seed, only tents. They took refuge in Jerusalem fearing Chaldean and Syrian armies. Brought into the LORD's house, they refuse wine, and through Jeremiah the LORD promises them a continuing line.

l: Jonadab the son of Rechab, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jonadab, son of Rechab, is father of the Rechabites; he commanded them never to drink wine, build houses, sow seed or plant vineyards, but live in tents; the LORD promises he will always have a man standing before him.

l: the LORD's house, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD's house is a place with multiple rooms serving as settings for key events. Jeremiah brings the Rechabites to the room of Hanan's sons, beside the princes' room, for the wine test. Later Baruch reads the scroll to the people on a fast day in Gemariah's room, since Jeremiah is barred from entering.

Wine is set before the Rechabites in bowls and cups at the LORD's command as a test, and they refuse it because of Jonadab's prohibition. Their refusal shows faithful obedience in contrast to Judah's disobedience.

l: Rechabite obedience to Jonadab's commands, The Book of Jeremiah
s: contrasts_with men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem [Judah has not listened to the LORD] The Rechabites have kept all of Jonadab's commands: no wine, no houses, no fields, vineyards, or seed, and life in tents, for them, their wives, sons, and daughters. The LORD holds this obedience up against Judah's failure to listen to him and rewards it with a promise that Jonadab will always have a man to stand before him.

A scroll holding the LORD's words against Israel, Judah and the nations, written by Baruch from Jeremiah's dictation; read publicly and to the princes, stored, then read to the king and burned, and replaced by a second, expanded scroll.

A group of officials including Elishama, Delaiah, Elnathan, Gemariah, and Zedekiah. They hear Micaiah's report, have Baruch read the scroll, fear, question him, tell him and Jeremiah to hide, store the scroll, inform the king, and three plead against burning it.

l: burning of the scroll, The Book of Jeremiah
s: While Jehudi reads to the king in the winter house, Jehoiakim cuts off three or four columns at a time with a penknife and throws them into the brazier until the whole scroll is consumed. He and his servants show no fear and do not tear their garments. The act leads to the LORD's command for a new scroll and his judgment on Jehoiakim.
Irijah, son of Shelemiah, is a guard captain at Benjamin's gate who seizes Jeremiah as a suspected defector, ignores his denial, and brings him to the princes.

l: princes (Judah's princes), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The princes are angry with Jeremiah when Irijah brings him before them. They strike him and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe, which they had made into a prison.

l: house of Jonathan the scribe, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jonathan the scribe's house, converted by the princes into a prison, holds Jeremiah in dungeon and cells for many days; he later begs Zedekiah not to return him there lest he die.

Ebedmelech is an Ethiopian eunuch in the king's house who trusts the LORD. He tells the king at Benjamin's gate that Jeremiah will starve in the dungeon, then leads thirty men to lift Jeremiah out with rags and cords. Later the LORD promises him deliverance from the sword and from those he fears, because of his trust.

l: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, is a governor appointed by the king of Babylon over the cities of Judah and the land. He settles at Mizpah, responsible for the poorest people left behind, and urges them to serve the Chaldeans for their well-being. He rejects Johanan's warning that Ishmael plans to kill him and forbids action. Hosting Ishmael and ten men at a meal in Mizpah, he is struck down and killed.

opposes Jeremiah [want him put to death for weakening the people] The princes, named as Shephatiah, Gedaliah, Jucal, and Pashhur, hear Jeremiah's words and ask the king to put him to death for weakening the men of war and the people. They throw him into the dungeon, and later question him about his talk with the king, but stop speaking with him when his answer matches the king's instruction and the matter is not perceived.

l: dungeon (Malchijah's dungeon), The Book of Jeremiah
s: Malchijah the king's son's dungeon, in the court of the guard, holds only mire, no water; Jeremiah is lowered by cords, sinks in the mire, and is later lifted out by Ebedmelech and thirty men.

l: Jeremiah's prophecy of Jerusalem's fall, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah's prophecy declares Jerusalem will be given to the king of Babylon's army. Those who stay die by sword, famine, and pestilence, while those who go out to the Chaldeans live. He repeats this privately to Zedekiah, promising survival and no burning if he surrenders; the capture remains pending.

Nebuzaradan is a captain of the guard serving Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. In the fifth month of the nineteenth year he enters Jerusalem and burns the LORD's house, the king's house and the great houses. He carries off the rest of the people, including deserters, and takes the temple's gold and silver. He leaves some of the poorest as vineyard keepers and farmers, giving them fields. He brings Seraiah, Zephaniah and others to Riblah for execution. On the king's command he takes Jeremiah from the court of the guard, releases him from his chains, acknowledges that the LORD brought the evil because of sin, offers him care in Babylon or freedom, and commits him to Gedaliah with food and a present. He later carries away 745 Jews in the twenty-third year.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The siege of Jerusalem was Nebuchadnezzar's military blockade of the city, in which he and his whole army built forts around it. It began on the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year and lasted into his eleventh year. By the ninth day of the fourth month famine was severe and bread was gone. A breach was made, the men of war fled by night, and Zedekiah fled and was captured. The houses were burned, walls broken, and survivors taken captive.

Mizpah is where Gedaliah dwells as governor and where Jeremiah goes to live with him. The captains, their men and returning Jews gather there, and it is where Johanan warns of the plot against Gedaliah. Mizpah was the place where Gedaliah was governor and where Ishmael killed him, the Jews with him, and the Chaldean men of war. Ishmael also killed pilgrims in the middle of the city and carried away the people remaining there as captives.

l: captains of the forces, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The captains of the forces and their men, who were in the fields, hear of Gedaliah's appointment and come to him at Mizpah, including Ishmael, Johanan, Jonathan, Seraiah, the sons of Ephai and Jezaniah. Gedaliah swears to them that serving the Chaldeans will go well, and Johanan with the captains later warns him of the plot. The captains of the forces join Johanan and the people in asking Jeremiah to pray to the LORD for the way they should walk. They are summoned with Johanan to hear the LORD's response.

l: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, is a royal descendant and chief officer who appears among the captains coming to Gedaliah at Mizpah. Johanan warns that Baalis of Ammon sent him to kill Gedaliah, but Gedaliah disbelieves it. Ishmael then arrives with ten men, eats with Gedaliah, and murders him, along with others at Mizpah. He deceives and kills eighty pilgrims and takes captives toward Ammon. Johanan overtakes him at Gibeon, frees the captives, and Ishmael escapes with eight men.

l: Johanan the son of Kareah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Johanan, son of Kareah, is one of the captains of the forces. He first warns Gedaliah at Mizpah of Ishmael's plot and privately offers to kill Ishmael, but Gedaliah forbids it. After Ishmael's crime, Johanan pursues him, finds him at Gibeon, and recovers the captives, though Ishmael escapes. He leads the remnant to Geruth Chimham, intending to go to Egypt out of fear of the Chaldeans. He and the people ask Jeremiah to seek the LORD's guidance. Yet he calls Jeremiah a liar, disobeys the LORD's voice, and leads the remnant, with Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt as far as Tahpanhes.

is_a king of the children of Ammon Baalis, king of the children of Ammon, is alleged by Johanan and the captains to have sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take Gedaliah's life. Gedaliah does not believe the report.

l: remnant of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: governed_by Gedaliah the son of Ahikam [set over them by the king of Babylon] The remnant of Judah consists of those not carried captive to Babylon, including men, women, children and the poorest, placed under Gedaliah. Johanan argues that Gedaliah's murder would scatter the gathered Jews and cause the remnant to perish.

l: plot to kill Gedaliah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Johanan and the captains report that Baalis, king of Ammon, has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take Gedaliah's life. Johanan offers to kill Ishmael secretly, but Gedaliah does not believe the report and forbids it.

l: eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Eighty mourning men from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, with shaved beards, torn clothes, and cuts, bring offerings and frankincense to the LORD's house. Ishmael meets them weeping, invites them to Gedaliah, then kills and pits them; ten are spared for hidden food stores.

l: people remaining at Mizpah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: includes king's daughters The people left in Mizpah, including the king's daughters, had been committed to Gedaliah by Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard. Ishmael carried them away captive toward the Ammonites, but they turned back and went to Johanan when he caught up at Gibeon. The recovered remnant included men of war, women, children, and eunuchs.

l: Geruth Chimham, The Book of Jeremiah
s: located_near Bethlehem Geruth Chimham, by Bethlehem, was where Johanan and the recovered remnant went and lived after leaving Gibeon. It served as their stopping point on the way to enter Egypt.

l: Gedaliah's assassination, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Ishmael son of Nethaniah and ten men kill Gedaliah with the sword at Mizpah after sharing bread, also slaying Jews and Chaldean soldiers; undiscovered for two days, it triggers more killings, captives, and fear of Chaldean reprisal.

l: remnant of Judah, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The remnant of Judah is a small surviving group, returned from the nations where they had been driven and living in the land. They ask the LORD for direction and swear obedience. The LORD tells them to stay, promising to build and plant them, and warns that Egypt means death. Jeremiah calls them deceitful. Johanan and the captains then lead everyone, including men, women, children and king's daughters, into Egypt, reaching Tahpanhes in disobedience.

l: this land (Judah), The Book of Jeremiah
s: will_be_built_up_for remnant of Judah [if they remain] The land is where the LORD says the remnant should keep living, promising to build and plant them there and not pull down or pluck up. The people's saying 'We will not dwell in this land' is described as disobedience to the LORD's voice. Going to Egypt means they will see this place no more.

located_in Egypt Tahpanhes in Egypt is where the remnant of Judah arrives after disobeying the LORD's voice. It is where the LORD's word comes to Jeremiah, and it contains Pharaoh's house, at whose entry the stones are to be hidden.

l: great stones, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah is commanded to take great stones and hide them in mortar in the brickwork at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes, in sight of the men of Judah. The LORD says he will set Nebuchadnezzar's throne on these stones, and the king will spread his royal pavilion over them.

l: Babylon's conquest of Egypt, The Book of Jeremiah
s: A prophesied event in which Nebuchadnezzar, as the LORD declares, comes to strike Egypt; people meet death, captivity or sword by appointed fate, and Egypt's gods are burned and carried off, foretold through Jeremiah's stones at Tahpanhes.

l: Jews living in Egypt (Judah remnant), The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jews who settled in Egypt after leaving Judah, at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and Pathros, repeat their ancestors' sins by burning incense to the queen of the sky and refusing Jeremiah's message. The LORD declares they will be consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence, with only a few escapees returning to Judah.

l: women (of the Jews in Egypt), The Book of Jeremiah
s: burns_incense_to queen of the sky [claim to act with their husbands' involvement] The women stand in the great assembly that answers Jeremiah, and they argue that they made cakes and poured drink offerings to the queen of the sky with their husbands' knowledge. Jeremiah addresses them directly with the men, saying their vows are fulfilled by mouth and hand, and the LORD's word applies to them as well.

l: idolatrous incense burning and drink offerings, The Book of Jeremiah
s: provokes the LORD of Armies [to anger] Burning incense and pouring drink offerings to other gods, specifically the queen of the sky, is the abomination that provoked the LORD's anger in Judah and Jerusalem and continues in Egypt. The people vow to continue it, and Jeremiah says the LORD remembered it and could no longer bear it.

l: coming judgment (the LORD's breaking down and plucking up), The Book of Jeremiah
s: The LORD announces that what He has built He will break down and what He has planted He will pluck up, throughout the whole land. He says He will bring evil on all flesh, with Baruch alone singled out to escape with his life.

l: Baruch's lament (sorrow and weariness), The Book of Jeremiah
s: Baruch had cried, "Woe is me now!", saying the LORD had added sorrow to his pain and that he was weary with groaning and found no rest. The LORD answers it by telling him not to seek great things for himself and by promising him his life.

l: Pharaoh Necoh, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Pharaoh Necoh is a king of Egypt whose army camped by the Euphrates at Carchemish; later Egyptians dismiss him as a noise who missed his time, and the LORD vows to punish him and his followers.

l: army of Pharaoh Necoh, The Book of Jeremiah
s: located_at Carchemish [by the river Euphrates] The army of Pharaoh Necoh is called to prepare shield, horses, and spears for battle, but is dismayed, turns backward, and its mighty ones are beaten down and flee without looking back. They stumble and fall in the north by the Euphrates, and the mighty fall against one another.

l: Egypt's defeat at Carchemish, The Book of Jeremiah
s: defeated_by Nebuchadnezzar [fourth year of Jehoiakim] Egypt's army was struck by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish by the river Euphrates in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. The defeat is depicted as a rout in which the mighty stumbled and fell, and as a sacrifice the Lord GOD of Armies holds in the north country on a day of vengeance.

l: advancing army (the northern invader), The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_part chariots [also strong ones and wheels] The invader is described through the stamping of the hoofs of his strong ones, the rushing of his chariots, and the rumbling of his wheels. The noise leaves fathers unable to look back for their children because their hands are so feeble.

l: sword of the LORD, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The sword of the LORD belongs to the LORD. Asked how long until it is quiet and told to rest in its scabbard, it replies it cannot, since the LORD commanded it against Ashkelon and the seashore.

l: destruction of the Philistines, The Book of Jeremiah
s: cuts_off Tyre and Sidon helpers [every remaining helper] A coming day is announced to destroy all the Philistines and to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper who remains. The LORD himself will carry it out, and signs of it include Gaza's baldness, Ashkelon being brought to nothing, and the remnant of their valley cutting themselves in mourning.

has_followers priests and princes (of Chemosh) [will go into captivity with him] Chemosh, the god of Moab, will go out into captivity with his priests and princes together. Moab will be ashamed of him as Israel was ashamed of Bethel, and his people are called undone.

l: destroyer (of Moab), The Book of Jeremiah
s: attacks Dibon The destroyer will come on every city of Moab so that none escapes, and the valley and plain will perish. He has come up against Dibon and destroyed its strongholds, and he has fallen on Moab's summer fruits and vintage.

l: judgment of Moab, The Book of Jeremiah
s: The judgment has come on the plain country and all the cities of Moab, far or near, and Moab's horn is cut off and its arm broken. It includes terror, the pit, and the snare, with the year of visitation, and the chapter ends by saying that thus far is the judgment of Moab.

l: pride of Moab, The Book of Jeremiah
s: has_attribute great loftiness and arrogance Moab's pride, loftiness, and arrogance are said to have been heard of, and the LORD declares that its wrath and boastings are nothing and have done nothing. This pride, in magnifying itself against the LORD, is given as a reason Moab will be made drunk, become a derision, and be destroyed as a people.

Damascus, called the city of praise and the LORD's joy, is a place foretold to fall: it grows feeble, flees, and is seized by anguish, its young men and warriors die in its streets, and the LORD's fire devours Ben Hadad's palaces.

Hazor is a secure, gateless nation targeted by Nebuchadnezzar, who has planned against it. Its people are told to flee, its camels and livestock become plunder, and it ends as a perpetual desolation, a dwelling place of jackals.

l: nation from the north (against Babylon), The Book of Jeremiah
s: is_enemy_of Babylon [will make her land desolate] A nation comes up out of the north against Babylon, along with a company of great nations and many kings from the uttermost parts of the earth. They are expert archers, cruel and merciless, riding horses in array with a voice roaring like the sea. They make Babylon's land desolate, and the LORD stirs them up to carry out his purposes.

l: Babylon's destruction, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Babylon's destruction is the LORD's vengeance for its pride and treatment of his people. It is announced as already accomplished: bulwarks and walls fall, and the earth trembles at its capture. Fire, flood, and drying fountains follow with sudden force. Its land becomes a perpetual, uninhabited desolation like Sodom and Gomorrah, nations no longer flow to Bel, and the sinking of the book in the Euphrates seals it.

Seraiah, son of Neriah and chief quartermaster, accompanied King Zedekiah to Babylon in his fourth year, where Jeremiah charged him to read the book aloud, pray for desolation, and sink it in the Euphrates.

l: book (Jeremiah's book against Babylon), The Book of Jeremiah
s: Jeremiah wrote in this book all the evil that would come on Babylon. Seraiah is to read it in Babylon, then bind a stone to it and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates. Its sinking symbolizes Babylon sinking and not rising again.

l: destroyers (against Babylon), The Book of Jeremiah
s: Destroyers are sent by the LORD against Babylon, described as a destroying wind, strangers who winnow her, and men like locusts. They come from the north, and even if Babylon mounts to the sky they will reach her. They take her mighty men and break their bows.

l: temple bronze vessels, The Book of Jeremiah
s: Bronze vessels made by Solomon for the temple, including pillars, the sea, bulls and ministering utensils, were seized by the Chaldeans and carried to Babylon, their bronze too great to weigh.

Jehoiachin, king of Judah, is held captive in Babylon; in the thirty-seventh year Evilmerodach frees him, speaks kindly, elevates his throne above other kings, and provides him a daily allowance until death.

Evilmerodach, king of Babylon, in the first year of his reign frees Jehoiachin from prison, speaks kindly to him, raises his throne above other kings' thrones, and grants him a continual daily allowance for life.

This document is the book of Micah, a prophetic work delivered by Micah of Morasheth during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. The LORD is the central figure, acting as witness, judge, shepherd, and redeemer, while Micah serves as lamenting messenger. The people, rulers, priests, and prophets of Jacob and Israel are the main objects of the message. It opens with the LORD coming down in judgment. Samaria will become rubble, the wound reaches Judah and Jerusalem's gate, and Micah mourns while naming towns that will suffer captivity. Chapter 2 pronounces woe on those who plot evil and seize fields and houses; they reject the prophets and will be driven out, yet the LORD promises to gather the remnant of Jacob like sheep. Chapter 3 condemns rulers who hate good and devour the people, and prophets who prophesy for money, while Micah claims to be filled with the LORD's Spirit. It ends with the declaration that Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become rubble. The tone then turns to hope. Chapter 4 pictures a coming time when nations stream to the LORD's mountain, weapons become farming tools, and each sits secure under vine and fig tree. The LORD will gather the lame into a remnant and reign on Zion forever, though Zion must first go to Babylon before being redeemed, and gathered nations will be threshed. Chapter 5 promises a ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah with ancient origins, who will shepherd in the LORD's strength, be peace, and deliver the people from Assyria. The remnant is pictured as dew and as a lion, and the LORD will remove horses, chariots, witchcraft, and idols and take vengeance on disobedient nations. Chapter 6 is a courtroom scene before the mountains. The LORD recalls the exodus, Moses, Aaron, Miriam, and Balak and Balaam, and states what is good: act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with God. He then charges the city with dishonest scales and violence, and promises desolation for following Omri and Ahab's ways. Chapter 7 begins with lament that the godly have vanished and families betray one another. The speaker resolves to wait on the LORD, confessing sin and trusting in vindication, with rebuilt walls and people returning from Assyria and Egypt. It closes with a prayer for shepherding and praise of the LORD as the God who pardons iniquity, delights in loving kindness, and keeps his oath to Jacob and Abraham.

l: the LORD, The Book of Micah
s: The LORD, titled LORD of Armies and Lord of the whole earth, is the central figure of these records: the God of Zion and of Israel, who speaks through Micah as witness, judge, accuser, and redeemer. Most important is his dual character. He brings judgment on oppressors, corrupt rulers, false prophets, idolatry, witchcraft, and disobedient nations, yet he also pardons iniquity, delights in loving kindness, does not retain anger forever, and keeps the covenant truth sworn to Jacob and the fathers. The account begins with him dwelling in his holy temple and summoning witness against the peoples. He comes down to tread the high places, making mountains melt, and declares Samaria a rubble heap and evil reaching Jerusalem's gate. He then plans disaster against oppressors, charges his people with acting as enemies, and will not answer the rulers who cry to him because of their evil deeds. He speaks against prophets who lead the people astray and decrees that Zion will be plowed like a field. Judgment turns toward promise: he will gather Jacob and Israel's remnant like sheep, going at their head. He will judge between many peoples and strong nations, teach nations his ways, reign over the remnant of the lame and driven away on Mount Zion forever, and redeem Zion from enemies at Babylon. He will cut off horses, chariots, and strongholds, destroy idols and witchcraft, and take vengeance on nations that did not listen. He then calls the mountains and hills as witnesses and contends with Israel, recalling the redemption from Egypt and the sending of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. He states what he requires of man: justice, mercy, and humility. He accuses the city of dishonesty and violence and announces its wounding and desolation for its sins. The records close with the speaker waiting for him as the God of salvation, a light in darkness who will plead the case, execute judgment, and shepherd his people. He is praised as incomparable for pardoning, casting sins into the sea, and keeping his sworn promise.

l: Micah of Morasheth, The Book of Micah
s: Micah of Morasheth is a prophet who receives the LORD's word during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. He begins by lamenting judgment on both, going stripped and naked and wailing because the wound has reached Judah. He then declares himself full of power by the LORD's Spirit, and of judgment and might, to confront Jacob's disobedience and Israel's sin. He ends in personal humility: mourning a faithless land, acknowledging his own sin and the LORD's indignation, yet waiting for the God of salvation, expecting light in darkness and rising after a fall.

has_wounds incurable [her wounds have reached Judah] Judah's kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah mark the time of the vision. Its high places are identified with Jerusalem. Samaria's incurable wounds are said to have reached Judah, coming to the gate of the LORD's people.

Samaria is identified as the disobedience of Jacob and the vision's focus. It is doomed: the LORD will turn it into a rubble heap like a vineyard planting place, spill its stones into the valley, expose its foundations, and smash its idols and burn temple gifts.

Jerusalem is a city tied to Judah's high places. It first appears alongside Samaria in a vision, where the LORD's incurable wound and evil reach its gate. It is then condemned as built with iniquity, with leaders, priests and prophets corrupted by money, and doomed to become rubble. Finally it is the source of the LORD's word and seat of restored dominion.

Jacob, the house of Israel, is a collective addressed in judgment: its disobedience, tied to Samaria, justifies coming judgment; it is questioned about the LORD's anger, promised full assembly, and its heads are summoned to know justice as its sin is declared.

Israel is the LORD's people, portrayed as a flock and heritage dwelling by themselves in a forest, and as a land. The records show it accused through its rulers of abhorring justice and perverting equity, and of keeping the statutes of Omri and the works of Ahab's house. The LORD contends with it, recalling redemption from Egypt and the Balak and Balaam episode. Judgment comes: it is besieged, its judge struck on the cheek with a rod, its horses, chariots, cities and strongholds cut off, and the land left desolate because of its inhabitants' deeds. Yet restoration is promised. The LORD will gather the remnant like sheep of Bozrah, with the king passing before them and the LORD at their head. They will feed in Bashan and Gilead as of old, have walls rebuilt and boundaries extended, be gathered from Assyria, Egypt and far places, and receive compassion, truth and mercy sworn to their fathers.

Zion is a place whose leaders judge for bribes and build it with blood, yet claim the LORD protects it from disaster. Because of their corruption it will be plowed like a field. It is also the source of the law and the mountain where the LORD will reign forever. The daughter of Zion must leave for Babylon, is rescued there, regains dominion, and receives an iron horn and bronze hoofs to thresh many peoples.

l: Judgment on Samaria and Judah, The Book of Micah
s: The LORD's judgment descends because of Jacob's disobedience and Israel's sins: mountains melt, Samaria is reduced to rubble with idols destroyed, then the incurable wound spreads to Judah and Jerusalem's gate, afflicting towns like Lachish, and children go into captivity.

l: those who devise iniquity (oppressors), The Book of Micah
s: Oppressors who plan evil on their beds and carry it out at morning light because they have the power. They covet and seize fields and houses, oppressing a man, his house and his heritage, including the LORD's people. They have no one dividing land by lot in the LORD's assembly. The LORD declares disaster against them, and they will be mocked with a lament.

l: my people (the LORD's people), The Book of Micah
s: The LORD's people, treated as a group, are first accused of acting as an enemy: stripping passersby returning from battle, driving women from their pleasant houses, and taking blessing from children. They are told to depart, as this is not their resting place, and favor a false prophet. Later they appear as victims, brutalized by rulers and misled by prophets proclaiming peace for those who feed them.

l: disaster (planned by the LORD), The Book of Micah
s: has_effect necks cannot be removed [people will not walk haughtily] The LORD says he is planning a disaster against the oppressors, from which they will not remove their necks. It makes them unable to walk haughtily, since it is an evil time. In that day they will lament that they are utterly ruined and that their fields are assigned to traitors.

l: heads and rulers of Jacob/Israel, The Book of Micah
s: The heads and rulers of Jacob/Israel, who should know justice, instead hate good, love evil, abhor justice and pervert equity. They oppress the LORD's people, building Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity, so the LORD will not answer their cry.

The prophets are a group who lead the LORD's people astray, proclaiming peace to those who feed them and preparing war against those who don't, while telling fortunes for money. As punishment, they receive night, no vision and darkness; seers and diviners are confounded, cover their lips, and get no answer from God.

l: coming destruction of Zion and Jerusalem, The Book of Micah
s: The LORD declares judgment on corrupt leaders: Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem become rubble heaps, and the temple mountain turn into forest high places, answering the leaders' false assurance that no disaster would come.

l: mountain of the LORD's temple, The Book of Micah
s: The LORD's temple mountain will, in the latter days, be established above all mountains and exalted above the hills, drawing streaming peoples and many nations who go up to be taught the God of Jacob's ways.

The nations are a collective of peoples portrayed with divided fates. Many will stream to the LORD's mountain to learn his ways, be judged, and abandon war. Yet each walks in its own gods' name, and some assemble against Zion to defile her, not knowing the LORD's counsel. He gathers them like sheaves for threshing, Zion beating many in pieces. The remnant of Jacob lives among them like a lion, and the LORD executes vengeance on those who did not listen.

is_place_of rescue of Zion [the LORD will redeem her there from enemies] Babylon is the place Zion will come to after leaving the city and dwelling in the field. There the LORD will rescue and redeem her from the hand of her enemies.

l: remnant of Jacob, The Book of Micah
s: The remnant of Jacob is the lame, driven away, and afflicted whom the LORD gathers. He makes the cast-off a strong nation and reigns over them on Mount Zion forever. Among many peoples the remnant is like refreshing dew and showers independent of man; among the nations it is like a lion, treading down and tearing in pieces with no deliverer. It returns to the children of Israel, its brothers.

l: swords and spears turned to farming tools, The Book of Micah
s: are_made_from swords and spears [beaten into plowshares and pruning hooks] When the LORD judges between many peoples and strong nations, they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will not lift sword against nation, nor learn war any more, and everyone will sit unafraid under vine and fig tree.

l: Bethlehem Ephrathah, The Book of Micah
s: Bethlehem Ephrathah, a small clan of Judah, is addressed as insignificant in size, yet from it a ruler in Israel will come forth for the LORD.

l: ruler in Israel, The Book of Micah
s: A ruler in Israel, coming from Bethlehem Ephrathah, whose origins are from ancient times. He shepherds in the LORD's strength and majesty, with the LORD as his God, becomes great to earth's ends, is peace itself, and delivers the people from Assyria's invasion.

has_land land of Nimrod [ruled by Israel's leaders with the sword] Assyria is described as invading the land and marching through its fortresses. In response seven shepherds and eight leaders of men will be raised against it, and they will rule the land of Assyria with the sword and the land of Nimrod in its gates. The ruler will deliver the people from the Assyrian.

l: idolatry and witchcraft, The Book of Micah
s: The LORD says he will destroy witchcraft from the people's hand and leave them no soothsayers. He will also cut off engraved images and pillars so that they no longer worship the work of their hands, and will uproot the Asherah poles.

l: the LORD's case against Israel, The Book of Micah
s: has_witness mountains and hills (the LORD's witnesses) [plead before them] The LORD summons Israel to plead before the mountains and hills and calls the enduring foundations of the earth to hear his indictment. He bases it on his saving acts, asks what he has done to burden them, and charges them with wickedness, dishonest scales, violence, lies, and following the ways of Omri and Ahab's house.

l: offerings and sacrifices, The Book of Micah
s: A speaker asks whether burnt offerings, year-old calves, thousands of rams, tens of thousands of rivers of oil, or even a firstborn child could win the LORD's favor. The answer given is not a sacrifice but a statement of what is good, which implies these are not what the LORD requires.

l: what the LORD requires (justice, mercy, humility), The Book of Micah
s: The text says the LORD has shown humanity what is good and that he requires three things: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God. This is given in answer to the question about offerings.

l: the city, The Book of Micah
s: A city addressed by the LORD's voice, where wisdom fears his name yet dishonest commerce thrives: wicked treasures, short ephah, false weights. It follows Omri's and Ahab's ways, speaks lies, and is threatened with ruin and hissing.

l: dishonest commerce, The Book of Micah
s: The LORD asks whether he can tolerate treasures of wickedness, an accursed short ephah, dishonest scales, and a bag of deceitful weights. These practices are named among the sins for which the city is punished.

l: rich men of the city, The Book of Micah
s: are full of violence [also speak lies] The rich men of the city are described as full of violence. Their inhabitants speak lies and have deceitful tongues, and these are among the grounds for the LORD's judgment.

l: the LORD's punishment, The Book of Micah
s: The LORD's punishment of the city for its sins: he declares it struck with a grievous wound and desolate, then foretells futility in eating, storing, sowing, and pressing olives and grapes, with savings lost to the sword, ending in the city becoming a ruin, a hissing, and a reproach.

l: wicked men of the land, The Book of Micah
s: The wicked men of the land are marked by ungodliness, with no godly or upright person left. They lie in wait for blood, hunt one another with nets, and diligently do evil, while rulers and judges demand bribes. Even their best are like thorn hedges. Their day of visitation and confusion arrives, leaving the land desolate.

l: enemy (who said 'Where is the LORD your God?'), The Book of Micah
s: An enemy, called 'her', taunted 'Where is the LORD your God?' over the speaker's fall. The speaker says he will arise, and expects her to witness the LORD's vindication, then be covered with shame and trodden down like street mire.

l: restoration and regathering, The Book of Micah
s: A promised future day of restoration: walls built and boundaries extended, people streaming from Assyria, Egypt's cities, the River, and sea to sea. The LORD shows marvels as in the exodus, and shamed, silenced nations come trembling in fear.

l: Israel's sins and God's forgiveness, The Book of Micah
s: A passage on Israel's sins and divine forgiveness: the speaker confesses sin and bears the LORD's indignation until he pleads his case, then praises a pardoning God who does not stay angry, will again show compassion, tread iniquities underfoot, and cast sins into the sea.

The Book of Nahum, in three chapters, is a prophetic oracle against Nineveh delivered through Nahum the Elkoshite. The central figures are the LORD, portrayed as a jealous, avenging yet slow-to-anger God who shelters those who trust him; Nineveh, the bloody city and its king of Assyria, who face judgment; and Judah, who receives good news. Chapter 1 establishes God's power over nature and his role as stronghold and avenger, promises to break the yoke from one addressed party, and pronounces doom on another, whose name, idols, and line will be cut off. It closes with a messenger announcing peace and telling Judah to keep its feasts and vows because the wicked one is cut off. Chapter 2 turns to the assault: an attacker with red shields and flashing chariots storms Nineveh, the river gates open, the palace dissolves, people flee, and the city is plundered and left empty. The lions' den is mourned, and the LORD of Armies declares he is against Nineveh. Chapter 3 pronounces woe on the city for lies, slaughter, prostitution, and witchcraft, promises public shame, and compares Nineveh to No-Amon, which fell despite its allies. Fortresses fall like ripe figs, fire and sword devour, and the king of Assyria suffers an incurable wound, welcomed by clapping because of his endless cruelty.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Nahum
s: The LORD of Armies is portrayed as a jealous, avenging God who is slow to anger, great in power, and good. He maintains wrath against his adversaries, rebukes the sea and commands storm and rivers, yet is a stronghold in the day of trouble who knows those taking refuge in him. In chapter 1 he promises to break Judah's yoke, afflict it no more, restore Jacob's excellency, and cut off the gods and images of Nineveh. In chapters 2 and 3 he declares himself against Nineveh: he will burn her chariots, let the sword devour her young lions, end her messengers' voice, expose her nakedness and shame before the nations, and make her a spectacle.

Nineveh is a city, the subject of Nahum's vision, portrayed as a bloody city full of lies, robbery, endless cruelty, prostitution and witchcraft that sell nations and families. Most important is that the LORD of Armies stands against it and decrees its ruin. The records unfold in three stages. First, the book opens with the revelation, and oracles foretell no more descendants bearing its name, its images cut off from its gods' house, and a grave made because it is vile. Second, it is told to prepare defenses but is overwhelmed: river gates open, the palace dissolves, people flee, silver and gold are plundered, and it is left empty, void, and waste, though it was long like a pool of water. Third, its shame is exposed and it becomes a spectacle. Its fortresses fall like ripe figs, its troops are women, its gates stand open, its merchants as numerous as stars and its guards like fleeing locusts cannot save it, and fire and sword devour it with no one to mourn. Its wound is fatal, with no healing.

will_be_free_of the wicked one [will no more pass through it] Judah is told to keep its feasts and perform its vows, because the wicked one will no more pass through it and is utterly cut off. A messenger bringing good news and publishing peace is seen on the mountains. The promise that the LORD will break the yoke and bonds and afflict "you" no more may also concern Judah, though the text does not name the addressee.

l: adversaries of the LORD, The Book of Nahum
s: The adversaries of the LORD are his enemies and those who plot against him. He takes vengeance, pursuing them into darkness and ending their place with a flood. Though strong and numerous, they are likened to thorns, drunkards, and dry stubble, and are cut down and consumed utterly, so affliction will not recur.

l: he who dashes in pieces (the attacker of Nineveh), The Book of Nahum
s: An attacker who comes up against Nineveh, equipped with red shields, scarlet-clad valiant men, and flashing chariots. His chariots rage through the streets like torches; his picked troops rush the wall and set up the shield. The assault ends in the city's collapse and plunder.

l: lion (Nineveh's den), The Book of Nahum
s: Nineveh's lion den is portrayed as a secure place where the lion, lioness and cubs lived unafraid, filled with torn prey. The text then asks where it is now, and the LORD of Armies declares the sword will devour the young lions and cut off their prey.

l: fall of Nineveh, The Book of Nahum
s: The fall of Nineveh is a foretold destruction framed by the LORD of Armies declaring he is against the city. It begins with an assault: chariots in the streets, river gates opened, the palace dissolving. The city is uncovered and carried away, its people flee and treasure is plundered, leaving it waste. Fortresses fall like ripe figs, gates stand open, fire and sword devour it, officials scatter like locusts, and its wound is incurable.

No-Amon is a place set among rivers, with the sea as its rampart and wall, and with Cush, Egypt, Put, and Libya as strength and helpers. It serves as a comparison for Nineveh: despite these defenses, it was carried into captivity, its children dashed in pieces and its great men chained.

l: king of Assyria, The Book of Nahum
s: The king of Assyria is addressed directly: his shepherds and nobles slumber, his people lie scattered on the mountains ungathered, and his wound is fatal and incurable, so all who hear of it applaud because of his endless cruelty.

l: Nineveh's violence and bloodshed, The Book of Nahum
s: The chapter opens with images of violence: the whip, rattling wheels, prancing horses, bounding chariots, charging horsemen, flashing swords, glittering spears, and endless heaps of corpses over which people stumble. The city is accused of lies and robbery with no end to its prey, and the king of Assyria's endless cruelty is felt by all.

The Book of Habakkuk is a three-chapter prophetic text centered on the prophet Habakkuk and the LORD, with the Chaldeans as the instrument of judgment. In chapter 1, Habakkuk cries out against violence, iniquity, and perverted justice. The LORD answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans, a fierce, feared nation whose strength is its god. Habakkuk affirms the LORD's everlasting nature but questions why one too pure to look on evil tolerates treachery, and he likens the oppressor to a fisherman who nets people and kills nations without mercy. In chapter 2, Habakkuk takes a watchman's post to await an answer. The LORD tells him to write the vision on tablets and wait, for it will surely come and the righteous will live by faith. A series of woes follows against the plundering, arrogant man, those who shame neighbors, and idol makers who trust lifeless wood, stone, gold, and silver. The chapter ends with the earth filled with knowledge of the LORD's glory and all the earth silent before him in his holy temple. Chapter 3 is Habakkuk's prayer, set to music. He asks the LORD to renew his work and remember mercy, recalls God's awesome coming from Teman and Mount Paran, and describes God saving his people and crushing the land of wickedness. Though trembling and waiting for the day of trouble, Habakkuk resolves to rejoice in the LORD even if crops and flocks fail, declaring that God is his strength and enables him to walk in high places.

Habakkuk is a prophet who calls the LORD his God. He begins by crying out over violence, injustice, and the failure of justice, then questions why the LORD tolerates treachery and whether the oppressor will keep killing nations. He stands at his watch on the ramparts awaiting the LORD's reply and is told to write the vision plainly on tablets. In his closing prayer he stands in awe of the LORD's deeds, trembles in body and lips, and waits quietly for the day of trouble. He nevertheless resolves to rejoice in the LORD even amid famine, and is given deer's feet to go in high places.

The LORD, also called LORD of Armies, is portrayed in the Book of Habakkuk as eternal, holy and too pure to look on evil, dwelling in his holy temple. In Chapter 1, Habakkuk accuses him of not hearing or saving, and he answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans to judge and punish. In Chapter 2, he tells Habakkuk to write the vision and wait, pronounces woes on the oppressor, promises the earth will fill with knowledge of his glory, and calls all the earth to silence. In Chapter 3, he is praised as coming from Teman and Mount Paran, shaking the earth, marching in wrath, and going out to save his people and anointed by crushing wickedness. Habakkuk asks him to remember mercy in wrath and declares him his strength and the God of his salvation.

The Chaldeans are a bitter, hasty, feared nation that the LORD raises up in Habakkuk 1. They march across the earth seizing dwellings not theirs, with swift horses and horsemen, scoffing at kings and strongholds, gathering prisoners like sand, and killing nations without mercy. They are declared guilty because their strength is their god and they trust in their net, yet they are appointed for judgment and punishment.

surround the righteous The wicked surround the righteous, so that justice comes out perverted. Habakkuk complains that the LORD keeps silent while the wicked swallows up a man more righteous than he, and he describes the oppressor netting people like fish, rejoicing, sacrificing to his net, and living luxuriously by it.
The righteous are a group surrounded and swallowed up by the wicked, perverting justice while the LORD stays silent, yet they are defined as those who live by faith.

Habakkuk cries out about violence, iniquity, perversity, destruction, strife, and contention, which are before him. He says the law is paralyzed and justice never prevails, and the Chaldeans are said to come all of them for violence.

An arrogant, puffed-up, treacherous man, insatiable like Sheol, who gathers and plunders nations through extortion and bloodshed. He is condemned with repeated woes. The peoples mock him with a taunting proverb, the plundered rise to plunder him in return, and he finally drinks the LORD's cup, exposed and covered in disgrace.
A vision written plainly on tablets for easy reading, meant for an appointed time; it hurries toward the end, will not prove false, and will surely come without delay, so one must wait.

labor_for fire [from the LORD of Armies] The nations and peoples have been plundered and gathered up by the oppressor, but the remnant of the peoples will plunder him in return. The text says they labor for the fire and weary themselves for vanity, and that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD's glory.

Idols are mute, breathless images overlaid with gold and silver, called worthless teachers of lies. Chapter 2 condemns makers who trust them and those who bid wood awake, contrasting them with the LORD in his holy temple.

is_done_to Lebanon [will overwhelm the oppressor] Men's blood and violence done to the land, cities, Lebanon, and the animals are named as the grounds on which the oppressor will be plundered and overwhelmed. The text condemns building a town with blood, and says the stone and beam of the house will cry out in witness.

The nations tremble when the LORD looks at them, and he threshes them in anger as he marches through the land in wrath. The ancient mountains crumble and the age-old hills collapse before him. The tents of Cushan are seen in affliction and the dwellings of Midian tremble.

The LORD goes out for the salvation of his people and his anointed. Habakkuk, speaking for them, says he must wait quietly for the day of trouble, when the people who invade them come up. The invaders' warriors come like a whirlwind to scatter them, but are pierced with their own spears.

includes failing fig tree and vines Habakkuk describes a possible famine in which the fig tree does not flourish, there is no fruit on the vines, the olive crop fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and the stalls hold no herd. Even in such lack, he says he will rejoice in the LORD and be joyful in the God of his salvation.

A prayer by Habakkuk the prophet, addressed to the LORD and set to victorious music for the music director on stringed instruments. It begins with pleas for renewed work and mercy, moves through a vision of God's powerful victorious coming, then Habakkuk's fear, ending in joyful trust in the LORD.

The Book of Zephaniah, in three chapters, records a prophetic message from the LORD to Zephaniah in the days of Josiah, king of Judah. Its central figures are the LORD, who judges and then restores, Judah and Jerusalem, the surrounding nations, and the humble remnant. Chapter 1 announces sweeping judgment: the LORD will clear everything from the earth, cut off Baal worship and those who turned from him, and punish princes, the king's sons, the violent, and the complacent in Jerusalem. The day of the LORD is portrayed as wrath, darkness, and alarm, when silver and gold cannot save anyone and the land is consumed by the fire of his jealousy. Chapter 2 urges the humble to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility before his anger arrives. It then pronounces destruction on the Philistine cities, Moab and Ammon, the Cushites, and Assyria, whose carefree capital Nineveh, claiming 'I am, and there is no one besides me,' becomes a desolation. Judah's remnant will inherit the conquered lands. Chapter 3 denounces the rebellious, polluted city and its corrupt princes, judges, prophets, and priests, though the LORD within her is righteous. After he gathers the nations in indignation, he will purify the peoples' lips, remove the proud, and leave a humble remnant living without lies or fear. The book ends with the daughter of Zion told to sing, because the LORD saves, rejoices over her, gathers the scattered, and restores their fortunes with honor and praise.

l: the LORD, The Book of Zephaniah
s: The LORD is the God of Israel and its king, who speaks to Zephaniah in the days of Josiah. He is righteous, doing no wrong and bringing his justice to light every morning. The records open with sweeping judgment: he vows to sweep away everything and punish Judah and Jerusalem. He then urges the humble to seek him and destroys the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, the Cushites, and Assyria, while famishing the gods of the land and promising to restore the house of Judah. The records close with him gathering the nations, purifying lips, removing the proud, saving the lame and the driven away, and rejoicing over Zion with singing as a mighty savior.

Judah is ruled by King Josiah, son of Amon, when the word comes to Zephaniah. The LORD declares he will stretch out his hand against Judah and cut off the remnant of Baal and the idolatrous priests from it.

Jerusalem is a city addressed in Zephaniah. It is portrayed as rebellious, polluted, and oppressing: it does not obey, accept correction, or trust the LORD, and its leaders are corrupt. The LORD first threatens to search it and cut off Baal's remnant, with wailing heard throughout. Later he promises to remove the proud, take away her enemy, honor her, and be among her, so she can rejoice.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Zephaniah
s: The LORD says he will stretch out his hand against all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Those among them who worship the sky's army, swear by Malcam, leap over the threshold, or fill their master's house with violence and deceit are marked for punishment.

l: day of the LORD's judgment, The Book of Zephaniah
s: The day of the LORD is announced as near and hurrying greatly, a day of sacrifice, wrath, distress, ruin, darkness and gloom, when trumpet and alarm sound against fortified cities and silver and gold cannot save anyone. It then appears as an appointed time of fierce anger on a shameless nation, passing like chaff, while the humble may be hidden. It culminates with the LORD rising to the prey, gathering nations to pour out indignation, devouring all the earth with the fire of his jealousy, then purifying the peoples' lips and removing the proud from his holy mountain.

l: men settled on their dregs, The Book of Zephaniah
s: believes the LORD will do neither good nor evil [say in their hearts] These men say in their heart that the LORD will neither do good nor evil. The LORD says he will search Jerusalem with lamps to punish them, and that their wealth will be plundered, their houses desolated, and they will build houses and plant vineyards without enjoying them.

l: sinful men, The Book of Zephaniah
s: has_sinned_against the LORD Because they have sinned against the LORD, the LORD will bring such distress on men that they walk like blind men. Their blood will be poured out like dust and their flesh like dung, and neither silver nor gold will deliver them.

l: man and animal, The Book of Zephaniah
s: The LORD says he will sweep away man and animal, along with the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea, and the heaps of rubble with the wicked. He also says he will cut off man from the surface of the earth.
The LORD vows to utterly sweep away everything from the surface of the earth. He will cut man off from it, and the whole land will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy.
The Philistines, a sea-coast people called Canaan and the nation of the Cherethites, are warned of the LORD's word: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron will be destroyed, leaving shepherds' pastures.

l: house of Judah, The Book of Zephaniah
s: will_possess sea coast [remnant of the house of Judah] The remnant of the house of Judah will receive the Philistine coast as pasture and will lie down in the houses of Ashkelon in the evening. The LORD, their God, will visit and restore them.

Moab is a proud nation accused of reproaching the LORD's people and magnifying itself against their border; as judgment it will become like Sodom, a perpetual desolation of nettles and salt pits, plundered by the remnant.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Zephaniah
s: The children of Ammon are accused of reproaching the LORD's people and magnifying themselves against their border; as judgment they will become like Gomorrah, perpetual desolation of nettles and salt pits, inherited by the LORD's surviving nation.
The LORD will stretch out his hand against the north and destroy Assyria. Its fate is tied to the desolation of Nineveh.

Nineveh is a joyous, careless city that boasted 'I am, and there is no one besides me.' It will be made a dry desolation where animals lie and pelicans lodge, while passersby hiss and shake their fists.

l: humble of the land, The Book of Zephaniah
s: The humble of the land, who keep the LORD's ordinances, are urged to seek the LORD, righteousness and humility, in hope of being hidden on the day of anger.

are_gathered_by the LORD [for indignation] The LORD says he has cut off nations, leaving their battlements and cities desolate and uninhabited. He also states that he will gather the nations and kingdoms to pour on them his indignation and fierce anger, and that all the earth will be devoured by the fire of his jealousy. Afterward he will purify the lips of the peoples so they call on his name and serve him shoulder to shoulder.

has a remnant free of iniquity and lies [will feed, lie down, and be unafraid] The remnant of Israel is promised that it will not do iniquity or speak lies, no deceitful tongue will be found in its mouth, and it will feed and lie down with no one making it afraid. Israel is told to shout and be glad because the LORD, the King of Israel, is among them and has thrown out the enemy.

l: afflicted and poor people, The Book of Zephaniah
s: take_refuge_in the LORD [left among Jerusalem] The LORD says he will leave an afflicted and poor people among the city after removing the proudly exulting ones. They will take refuge in the LORD's name, and they form the remnant that will live without deceit or fear.

l: restoration of fortunes, The Book of Zephaniah
s: brings honor and praise among all peoples [for Jerusalem's people] The LORD promises that at that time he will bring the people in and gather them, giving them honor and praise among all the peoples of the earth. This will happen when he restores their fortunes before their eyes, reversing the shame of those who were lame and driven away.
